title: Discharges and a daughter
stem:
You are an F2 doctor on an elderly care ward. Four patients are going home this morning, and their hospital transport arrives at 11:00. Their discharge letters and medicines still need completing. It is 09:30.

A nurse tells you that Mrs Harris's daughter is waiting at the nurses' station. She wants to talk about the DNACPR decision the consultant made for her mother yesterday.
instruction: Choose the 3 most appropriate actions to take in this situation.

options.text: Talk to the daughter now and finish the discharges afterwards.
options.detailed: Her concerns matter, but a full conversation now could take 30 minutes or more, and four patients may miss their transport home.

options.text: Explain the DNACPR decision quickly at the nurses' station.
options.brief: Too rushed and too public for a sensitive conversation.
options.detailed: A brief explanation in a busy area isn't the right setting, and she is likely to have questions that need time.

options.text: Ask the F1 to talk to the daughter about the decision.
options.brief: Passes a sensitive conversation to someone less experienced.
options.detailed: The F1 may not know the reasoning or feel confident discussing resuscitation. It isn't a fair delegation.

options.text: Speak briefly to the daughter and agree a time to meet today.
options.brief: She knows she'll be seen, and you can give her proper time.
options.detailed: A brief introduction and a definite time shows her she is taken seriously. A DNACPR conversation needs time and privacy, which you can give her properly once the discharges are done.

options.text: Ask the nurse to tell the daughter you're too busy today.
options.brief: Dismissive, and delays a conversation she needs.
options.detailed: She has come in specifically and is entitled to a discussion. Turning her away without a time to meet is dismissive.

options.text: Ask the nurses to complete the discharge letters for you.
options.brief: Discharge letters and prescriptions are a medical responsibility.
options.detailed: Nurses may help with parts of the discharge process, but the letters and medicines need a doctor to complete them.

options.text: Finish the discharge paperwork in order of transport times.
options.brief: Patients will miss their transport if the paperwork isn't ready.
options.detailed: If the letters and medicines aren't ready by 11:00, patients may lose their transport and stay in hospital longer. Working through them in order is an efficient use of the next 90 minutes.

options.text: Ask the nurse in charge to book a quiet room for later.
options.brief: A private space matters for a sensitive discussion.
options.detailed: A conversation about resuscitation shouldn't happen at the nurses' station. Booking a room now makes sure one is available when you are ready.

explanation.issue: This tests how you balance time-critical tasks with a sensitive conversation, making sure both are done properly.
explanation.keyDetails: Transport is at 11:00. The DNACPR discussion is important but not time-critical within the next 90 minutes. A private space is needed.
explanation.reasoning: [D] acknowledges the daughter and sets a time, [G] meets the transport deadline, and [H] prepares a suitable setting. The distractors risk the discharges ([A]), rush the conversation ([B]), delegate it unfairly ([C], [F]), or dismiss her ([E]).
explanation.competing: [A] feels kind, but a full conversation can wait an hour and a half, whereas the transport can't.
